title: Make mercy your mosque
hook: make mercy your mosque, faith your prayer mat, honest earning your Qur'an (Majh ki Var M1, ang 140)

segments.voice: Yesterday, You are my father, and your line: you are my family. Who did you call? Today Guru Nanak speaks to a Muslim friend in the words of his friend's own faith. Day six hundred fifty-four.

Guru Nanak spent his life among both Muslims and Hindus. His lifelong companion, Bhai Mardana, was a Muslim musician. In the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak often speaks to people in the language of their own practice. To Hindus he talks about the sacred thread, the pilgrimage, the lamp. To Muslims he talks about the mosque, the prayer mat, the fast. And in one salok in Majh ki Var, he builds a whole mosque without using a single brick.
screen: `AMONG MUSLIMS AND HINDUS.` → `IN THE LANGUAGE OF THEIR PRACTICE.` → `A MOSQUE WITHOUT A BRICK.`

segments.voice: The salok is on ang 140. It goes, in effect: make mercy your mosque, faith your prayer mat, and what is honest and rightfully earned your Qur'an. Make modesty and good conduct your observances and your fast; so become a Muslim. Make good deeds your Kaaba, truth your guide, and good works your creed and your prayer. Let your rosary be whatever pleases Him. Then, Nanak, He will keep your honor. The word for mercy is mihar, kindness, compassion that flows downhill toward whoever needs it. Now, what is this doing? It would be easy to hear it wrongly, as Guru Nanak telling Muslims to give up their mosques. That's not what the text says, and it's not how Sikhs read it. Guru Nanak doesn't ask anyone to stop praying, fasting or going to the mosque. He's asking what all of it is for, and answering: mercy, faith, honest living, truth, good deeds. It's the same move he makes toward Hindus in Asa di Var, where he describes a sacred thread spun from compassion and contentment. He speaks to each tradition from inside its own words, never as a foil. For Sikhs, the same question turns right back on themselves. What makes a gurdwara a gurdwara? What is the turban for, the Ardas, the langar? The salok's answer applies to every house of worship: the building matters, but mercy is what makes it holy. A person can kneel on the finest prayer mat in the world, or bow before the Guru Granth Sahib, and still need to ask whether mercy came in with them.
screen: `MIHAR: MERCY, COMPASSION.` · `MERCY THE MOSQUE, FAITH THE MAT.` · `NOT GIVING IT UP: FILLING IT.` · `THE QUESTION TURNS BACK ON SIKHS.` · then, large: `MERCY IS THE MOSQUE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Think of the place where you pray, or rest, or go to find quiet: a mosque, a gurdwara, a church, a bench by a lake, your own bedroom. Picture walking in. Now ask Guru Nanak's question: did mercy come in with me? Then think of one merciful act you could do today, small and real: a patient answer, a meal shared, a debt forgiven, a kind word to someone struggling. If you pray, you can say Waheguru and hold that act before the One. The bell holds the time.
Make mercy your mosque. Guru Nanak, speaking in Islam's own words: mercy the mosque, faith the prayer mat, honest living the Qur'an.
Your line: mercy is the mosque. Today, do one merciful act before you enter any place you call holy, or before you sleep. Day six hundred fifty-four.

screen: `DAY 654 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: YOU SPENT THE NIGHT SLEEPING.`

howItsDone: Sikhs sing and recite Majh ki Var in the gurdwara, and often cite this salok of Guru Nanak as teaching that every outward practice is fulfilled through mercy, faith and honest living.

fork.setup: you're Guru Nanak, speaking to a Muslim friend about prayer. what do you say?
options: make mercy your mosque and faith your prayer mat.
pray the way I do instead.
fork.reveal: he speaks inside his friend's own words, asking what each practice is for, never using it as a foil.

original.note: Gurmukhi: mercy, kindness; mihar maseet, mercy the mosque.

trapdoor: what you thought: Guru Nanak criticizing Islam.
what it means: Guru Nanak asking, in Islam's own vocabulary, what makes worship true: mercy, faith, honest living.

what a scholar hears: the salok maps virtues onto Islamic institutions point by point (maseet, musallaa, Qur'an, rozaa, Kaaba, kalmaa, nivaaj, tasbee), as Asa di Var does for the Hindu janeu; Sikhs read both as addressed to all, themselves included.
